validated_results.journal: Cancer epidemiology, biomarkers & prevention : a publication of the American Association for Cancer Research, cosponsored by the American Society of Preventive Oncology
validated_results.reason: Prospective cohort of 47,750 men assessing total, dietary, and supplementary calcium intake with incident prostate cancer outcomes, including a high versus low calcium intake relative risk for incident high-grade disease.

extraction.comparison_type: high versus low calcium intake (incident high-grade prostate cancer, Gleason >=7)
extraction.timing: dietary assessment in 1986, 1990, 1994, and 1998 with 16 years of follow-up
extraction.population: male health professionals with no history of cancer other than nonmelanoma skin cancer at baseline

sample_size.excerpt: We examined calcium intake in relation to prostate cancer risk using data from the Health Professionals Follow-up Study, a prospective cohort study of 47,750 male health professionals with no history of cancer other than nonmelanoma skin cancer at baseline.

cases.excerpt: Over 16 years of follow-up, we identified 3,544 total cases of prostate cancer, 523 advanced (extraprostatic) cases, and 312 fatal cases.

effect_size.excerpt: For high-grade prostate cancer (Gleason > or = 7), an association was observed for high versus low calcium intake (RR, 1.89; 95% CI, 1.32-2.71; P(trend) = 0.005), but a nonsignificant, inverse association was observed for organ-confined, low-grade prostate cancer (RR, 0.79; 95% CI, 0.50-1.25; P(trend) = 0.09).

confidence_interval.excerpt: For high-grade prostate cancer (Gleason > or = 7), an association was observed for high versus low calcium intake (RR, 1.89; 95% CI, 1.32-2.71; P(trend) = 0.005), but a nonsignificant, inverse association was observed for organ-confined, low-grade prostate cancer (RR, 0.79; 95% CI, 0.50-1.25; P(trend) = 0.09).

comparison.excerpt: For high-grade prostate cancer (Gleason > or = 7), an association was observed for high versus low calcium intake

validated_results.title: Meat consumption among Black and White men and risk of prostate cancer in the Cancer Prevention Study II Nutrition Cohort.
validated_results.journal: Cancer epidemiology, biomarkers & prevention : a publication of the American Association for Cancer Research, cosponsored by the American Society of Preventive Oncology
validated_results.reason: Prospective cohort reporting incident prostate cancer risk for cooked processed meat consumption among Black men with a quartile-based rate ratio and confidence interval.

extraction.comparison_type: highest versus lowest quartile of cooked processed meat intake (Black men)
extraction.timing: questionnaire in 1992 to 1993 with follow-up through August 31, 2001
extraction.population: Black and White men in the Cancer Prevention Study II Nutrition Cohort without a history of cancer

sample_size.excerpt: After excluding men with a history of cancer and incomplete dietary information, 692 Black and 64,856 White men were included in the cohort. During follow-up through August 31, 2001, we documented 85 and 5,028 cases of incident prostate cancer among Black and White men, respectively.

cases.excerpt: During follow-up through August 31, 2001, we documented 85 and 5,028 cases of incident prostate cancer among Black and White men, respectively.

effect_size.excerpt: Among Black men, total red meat intake (processed plus unprocessed red meat) was associated with higher risk of prostate cancer (RR, 2.0; 95% CI, 1.0-4.2 for highest versus lowest quartile; P(trend) = 0.05); this increase in risk was mainly due to risk associated with consumption of cooked processed meats (sausages, bacon, and hot dogs; RR, 2.7; 95% CI, 1.3-5.3 for highest versus lowest quartile; P(trend) = 0.008).

confidence_interval.excerpt: Among Black men, total red meat intake (processed plus unprocessed red meat) was associated with higher risk of prostate cancer (RR, 2.0; 95% CI, 1.0-4.2 for highest versus lowest quartile; P(trend) = 0.05); this increase in risk was mainly due to risk associated with consumption of cooked processed meats (sausages, bacon, and hot dogs; RR, 2.7; 95% CI, 1.3-5.3 for highest versus lowest quartile; P(trend) = 0.008).
